questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Smallest Vocal Unit That Carries No Meaning by Itself
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a sound unit from a meaning unit in a language
questions.stem: A speaker of a language produces a stream of sound with no pauses marking where one word ends and the next begins, yet other speakers of that language recover the words reliably. What is the smallest sound unit a speaker must control in order to do this?

options.text: A morpheme, since the smallest controllable unit is the piece that carries meaning and can be joined to others
options.misconception: calls the smallest contrasting sound unit the meaning-bearing piece, which is a different unit with a different job

options.text: A phoneme, since a word is built from a fixed small set of contrasting sound units that carry no meaning on their own
A word, since the recoverable unit must already be a whole word before a listener could locate its boundaries
options.misconception: insists the word must be found whole before its parts can be identified, which reverses the order of analysis

options.text: A syllable, since one syllable is the smallest unit a speaker could vary while keeping the utterance a single word
options.misconception: treats the syllable as the smallest contrastive sound unit, when contrasts exist well below the syllable

questions.explanation: The clue in the stem is that no pauses mark the boundaries, so the listener cannot be picking words out of gaps and must be using the sounds themselves. That requires the speaker to control contrasts that are smaller than a word, which is what a phoneme is: a member of the small set of sounds a language treats as distinct, and one that on its own means nothing. The unit that carries meaning is a morpheme, which is a different thing and often several phonemes long, so option B names a real unit of language but the wrong one for the job described. A word is not the smallest unit available, it is the output of the analysis, which is why C has the reasoning backwards. A syllable is larger than the contrasts that matter, since a single syllable routinely contains several phonemes, so D sets the floor in the wrong place.
questions.hint: Ask what the listener is using as evidence when no gaps are available to mark word boundaries.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: How Many Contrastive Sounds a Language Needs
questions.learningObjective: compute the lower bound on a sound inventory from a required number of contrasts
questions.stem: A language must be able to tell apart 44 different speech sounds using a code in which each sound is represented by a string of the same length made from just two symbols, and no two sounds may share a string. What is the smallest string length that makes this possible?
questions.explanation: This is a counting question before it is anything to do with psychology: with strings of length n over two symbols there are 2^n available strings, so the requirement 2^n at least 44 has to be satisfied. Two to the fifth is 32, which is short of 44, and two to the sixth is 64, which clears it, so six is the smallest length that works. The logarithmic route gives the same figure, since the base-two logarithm of 44 is 5.46 and a length must be a whole number, so six. The point worth keeping is what the number means and does not mean. Six is a floor forced by counting, not a measurement of anything: it says nothing about whether such a language exists, nothing about how its sounds are produced by the mouth, and nothing about which contrasts a particular community would find worth making. A language could carry far more than 44 contrasts, or exactly 44, and the bound is identical in both cases.
questions.hint: Work out how many distinct strings of length n can be built from two symbols, then find the smallest n that reaches 44.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Rule That Combines Sounds Rather Than Being One
questions.learningObjective: identify the unit of grammar and explain what it is not
questions.stem: English has roughly 40,000 dictionary entries and produces sentences no one has ever heard before, which is possible because the language has a rule for putting sound units together so that a small set of pieces yields a very large set of acceptable sequences. Which unit is that rule built out of?

options.text: Phonemes, because the productivity of a language comes from freely recombinable contrasts in sound
options.misconception: credits sound contrasts with the productivity that comes from recombining meaning-bearing pieces

options.text: Syntagms, because a grammar is a list of whole sentences held in memory and retrieved whole when needed
options.misconception: describes a store of whole utterances, which cannot produce a sentence never previously spoken

options.text: Morphemes, because each one is the smallest piece that carries meaning and a rule for ordering them builds new words from old
Sememes, because each one names a field of meaning and a rule for nesting fields builds sentences from them
options.misconception: invents an ordering principle over fields of meaning that no account of grammar relies on

questions.explanation: Two claims in the stem have to be satisfied at once, and the unit named in the right answer is the one that does both. A morpheme is the smallest piece that carries meaning, so a rule for arranging morphemes into words, and words into phrases and sentences, can produce a well-formed but never-before-heard sentence from a small inventory of pieces. Option A states that. Phonemes, which are the contrasting sound units, cannot be the source of the productivity, because rearranging sound units changes which word is produced rather than producing a new sentence, so B attributes the effect to the wrong level. A syntagm is a whole string that functions as a unit, and a language that stored whole sentences could not generate anything new, so C explains nothing. The final option names something that is not a standard unit of grammar at all, and nesting fields of meaning is not how sentences get built.
questions.hint: Ask which kind of piece can be rearranged to make a new sentence rather than a new pronunciation.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Kinds of Word Doing Two Different Jobs
questions.learningObjective: distinguish content words from function words by the work they do
questions.stem: In the sentence 'the child under the table ate a very large sandwich', the word 'the' appears once and 'ate' appears once, yet the two do different kinds of work in the sentence. What distinguishes them?

options.text: 'Ate' names an action and can stand alone in a short answer, while 'the' marks a role and cannot carry a reply by itself
'Ate' is a single syllable and 'the' is two, so syllable count is what separates the two kinds of word
options.misconception: makes syllable count the defining difference, which is an accident of the particular words chosen

options.text: 'The' appears earlier in the sentence than 'ate', and earlier words in English always do this job
options.misconception: treats word order in this one sentence as a general rule about which words mark roles

options.text: 'Ate' is a rare word and 'the' is a common one, so frequency is what puts them in different categories
options.misconception: uses how often a word is used as the criterion, which says nothing about its grammatical role

questions.explanation: The distinction that matters is whether a word can make a reply by itself, and only one of the two words in the sentence can. 'Ate' can: a question about what the child did can be answered with that word alone, because it names an event. 'The' cannot, because answering 'what did the child do' with 'the' tells the listener nothing; it can only mark that a noun phrase is coming and which role it plays inside it. That is why these are called content words and function words, and it is a division of labour rather than a difference of importance. The syllable option fails because the mapping between syllable count and category is coincidental in this sentence, and there are many-syllable function words and single-syllable content words. Word order fails because the two categories are identified by what they contribute, not by where they sit in one example. Frequency fails for the same reason: the most common words in any language are overwhelmingly the function words, and that is a consequence of the role rather than a definition of it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two words could be used on its own as an answer to a question about the sentence.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Same Words in a Different Order Asserting Something Else
questions.learningObjective: explain what word order contributes to meaning over and above word choice
questions.stem: In 'the boy chased the dog' the boy is the one doing the chasing, while in 'the dog chased the boy' the dog is. No word has changed and no meaning has been attached to a word; only the order has changed. What does this show about the relationship between word order and meaning?

options.text: Word order carries no meaning, because each word already carries a fixed meaning and nothing is contributed by the sequence
options.misconception: denies that order can contribute anything, having just read a reversed meaning off the same word set

options.text: Word order marks which words are old information and which are new, which is the only job order does
options.misconception: confines order to an information-structure role, ignoring the reversal of who did what

options.text: Word order determines which words are content words and which are function words, so the categories depend on position
options.misconception: makes word class depend on position, when the classes are fixed for these words

options.text: Word order carries part of the meaning, because the same words in a different order describe a different event

questions.explanation: The stem is built so that a single feature is varied and everything else is held constant: same words, same meanings, different order, different claim about the world. That isolates order as a carrier of meaning and rules out any account on which the words alone determine the message. Option A is that reading. Option B cannot be right, because it has to deny the very difference the stem displays; if order contributed nothing, the two sentences would mean the same thing, and they plainly do not. Option C picks a real job that order does do in many languages, marking what the listener is expected to treat as already known, but it is not the only job and it does not explain why the roles in this sentence swap. Option D is simply wrong about word class, since whether a word is a function word does not depend on where it stands.
questions.hint: Ask what was held constant between the two sentences, and what changed in what the sentences assert.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: One Pair of Words, Two Different Claims
questions.learningObjective: read the difference in claim between an active and a reversed clause
questions.stem: Four sentences are given. 'The apprentice repaired the clock.' 'The clock was repaired by the apprentice.' 'The apprentice was repaired by the clock.' 'The clock repaired the apprentice.' Three of these describe a repair in which the apprentice is the worker. Which statement about the fourth sentence is correct?

options.text: It is ungrammatical, because English does not allow a machine to occupy the subject position of a human worker
options.misconception: supposes a restriction on which sorts of nouns may fill a subject position, which English does not have

options.text: It describes a different event, in which the clock does the repairing, and the reversal is carried by word order alone
It means the same as the first sentence, because the subject and the object can be exchanged without changing the event
options.misconception: believes subject and object can be swapped freely, which would make the two sentences interchangeable

options.text: It has no meaning at all until a listener is told which reading is intended, so it is not a sentence with a content
options.misconception: treats a well-formed sentence as meaning-less until a reading is supplied, ignoring the conventional default reading

questions.explanation: Three sentences put the apprentice in the working role, and the fourth takes it away, which is exactly what the option that is correct describes. The point the sentence demonstrates is that the same two words in the opposite order assign the roles differently, and nothing about the words themselves changed to produce that. Option B fails because English puts all sorts of things in the subject position without complaint, and an implausible agent is still a well-formed sentence rather than a non-sentence. Option C fails because the whole demonstration is that the swap is not free; if it were, the sentences would be synonymous and there would be nothing to observe. Option D confuses the absence of a speaker's intention with the absence of meaning, since a listener recovers a conventional reading without being told, and the ability to say a second thing was meant is a separate matter from whether the sentence has content.
questions.hint: Ask which noun occupies the subject position in the fourth sentence, and whether that changes who is doing what.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Whose World a Set of Words Points At
questions.learningObjective: explain how a listener resolves a reference that the words leave open
questions.stem: A speaker says 'put the book on top of it' while holding a cup and looking at a shelf, and the listener puts the book on the shelf. Nothing in the words identifies what 'it' refers to, yet the reference is recovered. What supplies the missing information?

options.text: A fixed rule of the language, since a pronoun has exactly one referent once the sentence is well formed
options.misconception: claims each pronoun has a single obligatory referent, which would leave it useless in ordinary conversation

options.text: The speaker's private intention, since the listener can only resolve the reference by guessing what the speaker meant privately
options.misconception: puts the information in the speaker's unobservable intention, which the listener has no access to at all

options.text: The shared situation, since the words plus what both parties can see and hear together determine what a pronoun picks out
The dictionary, since a pronoun's referent is settled by the definition the dictionary gives for that pronoun
options.misconception: treats reference as fixed by lexical definition, ignoring how context selects among referents

questions.explanation: The stem's evidence is that the listener succeeds with information the words do not contain, so whatever does the work has to be something both parties have access to at the moment of speaking. A shared situation does exactly that, and this is the ordinary mechanism behind deixis, the class of expressions whose reference shifts with the context. Option A names it. Option B is refuted by the stem's own success: if a pronoun had one obligatory referent, the sentence would either be interpretable without any context or unusable, and it is plainly usable and plainly ambiguous on its own. Option C locates the information somewhere the listener cannot go, so it cannot explain how the listener got there, which makes it a description of what happened rather than a mechanism. Option D fails for the same reason in a different guise: a dictionary entry for a pronoun cannot settle which cup was meant in a particular utterance.
questions.hint: Ask what information was available to the listener that is not in the sentence.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: What a Speaker Means Beyond What Is Said
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what is said from what is meant and why the gap is systematic
questions.stem: Someone says 'that meeting was a bit long, then', in a setting where everyone knows the meeting was very long and everyone was suffering. The literal sentence is true on its narrow reading, but listeners hear a complaint. What is the linguistic name for the gap between the literal content and what is understood?

options.text: Phonology, because the extra meaning is carried by how the sounds are timed and stressed
options.misconception: assigns the inferred meaning to timing and stress, which shape delivery rather than supplying referents

options.text: Semantics, because the sentence must be read against the fixed dictionary sense of each of its words
options.misconception: insists the intended complaint is fixed by dictionary senses, ignoring the context entirely

options.text: Syntax, because the order of the words signals the speaker's attitude more strongly than the choice of words
options.misconception: reduces the effect to word order, which is unchanged between the literal and the felt reading

options.text: Pragmatics, because the difference lies in what the context licenses a listener to infer rather than in the words alone

questions.explanation: The stem describes a sentence whose literal content is correct and whose understood content is stronger, and asks what accounts for the difference. Nothing in the sound pattern or the word order differs between the narrow reading and the heard reading, so the extra content cannot be coming from either of those, which disposes of two of the options immediately. It comes from what the shared situation makes it reasonable to infer, and that is the subject matter of pragmatics. Option A says this. Option C fails because a fixed dictionary sense would give one content, not two, and the complaint is not in the entry for any of the words used. Option D fails because the order of the words is the same in both readings, so it cannot be what changed. The general lesson worth carrying away is that the gap is systematic rather than accidental, since listeners reliably reconstruct the stronger reading and reliably read the understatement as such.
questions.hint: Ask which layer of language would have to change for the difference to appear, and whether anything about the sounds or the order changed.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Part of an Utterance a Speaker Does Not Say Out Loud
questions.learningObjective: explain how an unstated assumption affects how an utterance is taken
questions.stem: A speaker says 'I will bring the drinks' after being asked who is helping. Everyone accepts that the speaker is not going to supply the whole party, even though nothing in the sentence limits what will be brought. How does that assumption work?

options.text: It is left unstated and reconstructed by the listener, and it shapes what counts as a sufficient answer
It is present in the sentence but stated more briefly than a full clause would be, so it is an ellipsis in the strict sense
options.misconception: claims a grammatical gap is present, when the sentence contains no elided clause to recover

options.text: It is carried by the speaker's tone, so a different delivery would remove it without changing a word
options.misconception: makes the assumption a function of delivery, which is not where unstated content lives

options.text: It is absent, because the question only asked who is helping and the answer fully satisfies the question as asked
options.misconception: denies that the answer leaves anything open, which is the assumption in question

questions.explanation: The stem's evidence is that everyone takes the answer as sufficient while nobody heard anything that limited the drinks, so the limitation is real, shared and not in the words. That is the signature of content the sentence leaves unstated and the listener supplies, and the supply is what makes the sentence an adequate reply to the question. Option A states the mechanism. Option B fails because there is no elided material to recover: nothing grammatical is missing, so this is not an ellipsis, and the restriction comes from the shared situation rather than from the sentence being a shortened version of a longer one. Option C confuses how unstated content is conveyed with how it is arrived at; the assumption would be available to a listener who could not see the speaker's face. Option D is the assumption in question restated as a conclusion, and the question does bear on quantity, which is exactly why the unspoken limit is doing work.
questions.hint: Ask whether there is any grammatical material missing from the sentence, and where the limitation on the drinks comes from.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Sounds a Speaker Makes That Are Not Words
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a speech sound from a sound made while producing speech
questions.stem: A recording is made of a person giving a spoken account of their week. It contains a click before the 'p' of 'people', a grunt before a shift of topic, and a short 'mm-hm' while another person is still speaking. How should these three sounds be classified?

options.text: The click is a phoneme of the language while the grunt and the 'mm-hm' are not, since only the click is produced inside a word
options.misconception: treats whether a sound sits inside a word as the test for being a member of the sound inventory

options.text: All three are speech sounds outside the word stream, produced by the speech apparatus and carrying no lexical content of their own
All three are words, since each one is a deliberate unit of communication with a conventional meaning
options.misconception: calls every intentional vocal signal a word, which would make any agreed gesture vocabulary into words

options.text: None of them are speech at all, since speech is by definition the production of words in sentences
options.misconception: restricts speech to sentences, which leaves ordinary conversation with pauses and overlaps undescribed

questions.explanation: All three sounds are made by the same apparatus that makes the words, they occur in the flow of speech rather than outside it, and none of them is a member of the language's inventory of contrasting sound units that a word is built from. Those three properties are what the correct option lists. The alternative that divides them fails because being inside a word boundary is not the test for being a member of the sound inventory, and because the grunt and the 'mm-hm' are in no sense less produced by the speech apparatus than the click is. The alternative that makes all three words fails because being a deliberate unit of communication is not sufficient for being a word, since a conventional agreed gesture carries meaning without being one, and none of these sounds has a lexical entry or takes part in the word-building rules. The alternative that excludes them all fails because it defines speech as sentence production, which would leave the great majority of real speech undescribed.
questions.hint: Ask what each sound shares with the words around it, and whether any of them has a place in the language's inventory.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Hearing Speech in Something That Is Only Noise
questions.learningObjective: explain what a speech perception demonstration does and does not establish
questions.stem: A recording is made by splicing together the parts of a recording of speech that carry no information about the message, including the parts that would let a listener track the pitch of the voice. Listeners report hearing the original message, and can do it for sentences they have never heard before. What does this show?

options.text: That listeners recover messages from the smallest possible cues, since whatever survives a cut of this size must be sufficient on its own
options.misconception: concludes the surviving cues are sufficient in isolation, without checking whether the original message was still recoverable

options.text: That comprehension is entirely a matter of acoustic analysis, since no meaning was supplied by a speaker
options.misconception: removes the listener's knowledge of the language as a possible contributor to the result

options.text: That the message can be recovered from cues the experiment left in, which is a fact about the stimuli rather than a proof of any one mechanism
That the listeners were guessing systematically from the grammar alone, since the acoustic cues were removed
options.misconception: treats listeners as ignoring the stimuli rather than using them, which the novel sentences argue against

questions.explanation: The demonstration is a real and striking one, but what it licenses is narrower than the interpretation usually attached to it, and the stem supplies the reason. Listeners recover the message for sentences they have never heard, which means they are not reciting something stored, so they must be using something in the recording. But nothing in the result identifies which cues carried the message, and the experiment was not designed to establish that the surviving cues would be sufficient without the rest of the original signal, so the cautious reading in the right option is the defensible one. The option claiming sufficiency claims more than the design tested. The option excluding a contribution from the listener's knowledge removes a source that is available and that a demonstration like this cannot remove. The option that has listeners guessing from grammar alone would require them to be ignoring the recording, which is the opposite of what they are reported to be doing, since novel sentences cannot be guessed from grammar.
questions.hint: Ask what the experiment measured and what it did not measure about the surviving cues.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Fitting an Unfamiliar Word Into a Familiar Shape
questions.learningObjective: explain how a novel sound pattern is sorted into a known category
questions.stem: A listener hears a word that has not been heard before but which contains a familiar vowel surrounded by two consonants already in the listener's inventory. The listener places it in an existing word class within a second or so. What is being used to make that placement?

options.text: A complete analysis of every sound in the new word, so the word can be identified before it can be placed
options.misconception: reverses the order, claiming full identification is achieved first and classification follows

options.text: The dictionary, since the lookup of an unknown word yields its category directly without any perceptual work
options.misconception: treats dictionary lookup as the perceptual mechanism, which is what is being explained away

options.text: The speaker's intended meaning, since the listener uses the topic of the conversation to decide the category
options.misconception: makes the classification follow from the intended content, ignoring the acoustic cues the stem describes

options.text: The relationship of the new pattern to existing categories, so classification precedes full identification of the word

questions.explanation: The stem is arranged so the listener never gets to identify the word, yet does place it, and that ordering is the whole point. Classification on the basis of how a pattern relates to known patterns is available early, before the fine details needed for identification have been resolved, and it is what lets a listener follow speech at the speed speech arrives. That is the correct option. The alternative that puts a complete acoustic analysis first inverts the order and cannot explain how the placement happened in about a second on a word never heard before. The dictionary option is misplaced, since a lookup is a thing a listener does afterwards with a keyboard or a memory of definitions, not a perceptual mechanism operating in real time. The topic option identifies a real source of constraint on interpretation, which is why it sounds plausible, but the stem gives the listener the cues and no topic, so it cannot be what placed the word.
questions.hint: Ask whether the listener ever identified the word, and if not, what the placement could have been based on.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Tone of Voice Carrying Part of the Message
questions.learningObjective: explain a contribution that pitch and timing make to meaning
questions.stem: Four recordings of the same sentence are played: one flat, one sharply falling at the end, one sharply rising, one with the whole sentence pitched high. Listeners agree that the four do not convey the same attitude, though the words and their order are identical. What is being demonstrated?

options.text: That pitch and timing carry information about stance independently of the words, which is why the same sentence can be heard as agreement or as a challenge
That the words do not carry meaning at all, since changing the voice changes what is being said
options.misconception: concludes the lexical content is unreal, when only its delivery changed

options.text: That the listener is inferring a fixed attitude per speaker rather than responding to the delivery heard on that occasion
options.misconception: makes the response a stable trait of the speaker rather than a response to the stimulus

options.text: That prosody is the primary carrier of meaning and word choice is a secondary refinement added afterwards
options.misconception: sets a hierarchy between prosody and word choice that the demonstration does not establish

questions.explanation: The design holds the words and their order fixed and varies only delivery, and the listeners' judgements change with it. That is a clean isolation of a contribution that does not depend on the lexical material, and it is why a rising terminal can be heard as a question or as disbelief while the sentence itself is an assertion. The correct option says exactly this and does not overreach. The option denying that the words carry meaning cannot be right, since the listeners heard and responded to the words as well, and a change of delivery adds something rather than removing the lexical content. The option about fixed attitudes misdescribes the task: listeners were responding to recordings, and nothing in the setup gives them a history with the speakers from which to infer a disposition. The option ranking prosody above word choice sets up a comparison the design never performed, since no condition here removes or varies word choice.
questions.hint: Ask what was varied between the four recordings and what stayed the same.

questions.topic: Language: Recovering Sentence Structure While the Words Arrive
questions.learningObjective: describe what a listener must do during online sentence comprehension
questions.stem: A sentence is being heard word by word and the listener must decide, as each word arrives, which earlier words it attaches to. The situation is usually described as incremental parsing. What makes it hard?

options.text: The listener must store every word until the sentence ends, because no attachment is possible before the final punctuation
options.misconception: requires waiting for the end of the sentence, which is the opposite of what happens online

options.text: An early commitment may turn out to be wrong, and revising it costs time that the unfolding sentence does not allow
Each word can attach to exactly one earlier word, so the listener merely picks the nearest possible host
options.misconception: assumes a single possible host per word, removing the choice that makes the task difficult

options.text: Nothing is difficult, because the grammar of the language is fixed in advance and can be applied mechanically
options.misconception: treats grammar as a fully specified algorithm, leaving no room for error or revision

questions.explanation: Because the structure has to be built while the input is still arriving, a choice made on early evidence cannot be taken back without cost, and the cost is measured in reader time. That is the source of difficulty, and it is why sentences that are only clear in retrospect are hard in exactly this way. The correct option names that cost. The option requiring the listener to wait for the end describes a different and much slower process, and would predict no difficulty at all while the sentence is still unfolding. The option with a single possible host removes the choice that creates the problem, since a word with only one place to go cannot be misattached. The option calling the process mechanical leaves no room for the evidence that misanalysis occurs and is later repaired.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a listener who has attached a word to the wrong host, and whether the sentence gives time to correct it.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Point at Which a Sentence Proves to Have Been Misread
questions.learningObjective: interpret a misanalysis measure and what it does and does not index
questions.stem: Participants read sentences on a screen one word at a time, and the time taken at each word is recorded. Two kinds of sentence are used. On 60 garden-path sentences the proportion of readings that had to be revised was 12 out of 60. On 60 unambiguous control sentences the figure was 2 out of 60. Which conclusion does this pattern support?

options.text: That ambiguous sentences are harder to read, with no relation to revision at all, since the two revision figures are far apart
options.misconception: asserts no relation between the conditions and the revision rate while citing the very gap that supplies the relation

options.text: That a fifth of all readings had to be revised, since the two figures can be averaged to describe the whole set of sentences
options.misconception: averages two rates that were measured on separate kinds of sentence and calls the result a property of all reading

options.text: That revision was more often needed on the ambiguous sentences, which is what the manipulation predicts and what these two rates show
That revision is unrelated to ambiguity because 12 out of 60 is close enough to 2 out of 60 to be the same share
options.misconception: calls a sixfold difference between the shares the same, which it plainly is not

questions.explanation: Each rate has its own denominator, which is the set of sentences of that kind, and the comparison that matters is between them: 12 in 60 against 2 in 60, a sixfold difference. Since ambiguity was the only thing varied between the two kinds of sentence, that difference is what the manipulation predicts, and stating it in those terms is the strongest conclusion the data carry. The option denying any relation is self-defeating, since the gap between the two figures is the evidence for the relation. The option that averages is the classic denominator error: the two rates describe different populations of sentences, and their mean describes no population at all, and in any case the combined figure would be 14 in 120. The option calling the rates the same is a plain misreading of the arithmetic, because 0.20 and 0.033 are not close to each other.
questions.hint: Compute each rate against its own set of sentences, then ask what was varied between the two kinds.

questions.learningObjective: run and read a chi-square test on a 2x2 table of reading outcomes
questions.stem: In a reading study, 110 sentences were presented one word at a time. Of 50 sentences with an ambiguous structure, 38 were given the intended parse on the first pass and 12 were revised. Of 60 unambiguous sentences, 56 were given correctly first time and 4 were revised. Which statement about these data is correct?

options.text: A chi-square on the 2 by 2 table gives about 6.59 on 2 degrees of freedom, which exceeds 5.99 and so differs from chance
options.misconception: counts the degrees of freedom as the number of cells rather than as the excess rows over one times the excess columns over one

options.text: The revision rates differ but a chi-square is not needed, since any difference between two proportions settles the question by itself
options.misconception: treats any observed difference as decisive, which is the inference a test exists to avoid

options.text: The association is strong enough to show that ambiguity causes misreading, since the significant result identifies a direction of effect
options.misconception: reads a significant association as a demonstrated causal direction, which the design cannot deliver

options.text: A chi-square on the 2 by 2 table gives about 6.59 on 1 degree of freedom, which exceeds 3.84 and so differs from chance at the 5 percent level

questions.explanation: The computation is short. The four expected counts under independence are 50 times 94 over 110, and its three companions, giving 42.7, 7.3, 51.3 and 8.7. Summing observed minus expected, squared, divided by expected, over the four cells gives 6.59. The degrees of freedom for a 2 by 2 table are one, since that is one row fewer than the rows times one column fewer than the columns, and 6.59 on 1 degree of freedom has a p value a little above 0.01, which is below 0.05, and the critical value at that level is 3.84. That is the correct option. The option with 2 degrees of freedom uses a rule that does not apply to a two-row table and pairs it with the critical value from a two-row table, which is 3.84 and not 5.99. The option that skips the test asserts exactly what the test exists to avoid, since with any sample a difference can appear by chance. The option reading a significant association as a demonstrated cause is the error the design was built to avoid, since nothing here manipulated ambiguity.
questions.hint: Work out the four expected counts, then use one row fewer times one column fewer for the degrees of freedom.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: The Step From Making Sounds to Using a Word
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages that lead to a first word
questions.stem: Put these five steps in the order in which they occur on the way to a child's first word.

options.text: Babbling that uses the sound patterns of the language the child is learning
Joint attention, in which the child and a caregiver attend to the same object at the same time
A particular sound used with a consistent pattern so that a caregiver responds to it
The sound used to refer to a specific object, held in mind while it is out of sight
Further words, which arrive one at a time around that first referent

questions.explanation: The keyed order is A, C, B, D, E, and the reason for each position is what makes the sequence worth learning. Babbling comes first because it establishes the sound patterns of the language and appears well before any word means anything. A sound used with a consistent pattern to a caregiver comes next, because the child has by then separated the sounds of their language from the sounds of other languages, and the caregiver's contingent response makes one particular sound socially interesting. Joint attention follows that, and the ordering is not arbitrary: a word needs a shared focus for its referent to be fixed, and shared attention is what turns looking at something into referring jointly to it. Only then can a sound be used for a specific object, and using it for something out of sight is a further demand still, because the word now has to stand for an absent referent. The last step is that other words arrive around the first one, which is why a first word is usually a common noun and is often used to mean a whole phrase at first. Every distractor here is a valid step, and each one is wrong only in position.
questions.hint: Joint attention must fall after a sound has acquired social value and before a word can fix a referent.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Words That Arrive Before the Grammar Does
questions.learningObjective: interpret evidence that productive word use precedes grammatical mastery
questions.stem: A child of about two years produces utterances of two or three words, and the two-word combinations are drawn from a small closed set: wants, more, no, allgone, look, gone. What does the restricted set suggest about what the child has acquired so far?

options.text: A small set of whole phrases used as single units, with the underlying arrangement of subject and object still to be built
The whole grammar of the language at once, since a closed set of pairs is enough to generate every sentence
options.misconception: overreads a closed set as a complete generative system, which is the property the closed set lacks

options.text: No grammar at all, since a genuine grammar requires open-ended combination and a closed set cannot be one
options.misconception: concludes that no productive system exists, when a restricted one plainly does

options.text: A set of word meanings with no arrangement, so the pairs are simply two unrelated words spoken in sequence
options.misconception: denies that the pairs are structured, ignoring that a fixed order is what makes them phrases

questions.explanation: A closed set of pairs that recur in a fixed order is the signature of whole items stored and retrieved as units, which is a real and effective way of communicating, and it is the normal state of affairs at this age. What has not yet been developed is the open-ended arrangement that lets a child take a noun and a verb that never occurred together and make a novel and acceptable sentence, and the closed set is exactly the evidence that this is so. That is the correct reading. The alternative that credits a full grammar overreads: a closed set is the opposite of productivity, and a child with a full grammar would produce combinations that are absent from the list, which is precisely what is not observed. The alternative saying there is no grammar mistakes a restricted system for no system. The alternative treating the pairs as unrelated words cannot explain the fixed order, and a fixed order that recurs is structure.
questions.hint: Ask what a closed set of recurring two-word patterns implies about whether the pairs are stored as items or built from a rule.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Word Used for Something Not Presently There
questions.learningObjective: describe deferred reference and what a first word of this kind requires
questions.stem: A child says 'car' while alone in a room, looking steadily at a space on the floor where no car is visible to an observer. A second observer looking from another angle reports a toy car on a low shelf. Which description fits the evidence best?

options.text: The word is being used to refer to something outside the immediate field of attention, and the observers differ because the referent is not in view from both places
The word is being used to name whatever the child is looking at, so the referent must be a patch of empty floor
options.misconception: fixes the referent at whatever occupies the gaze, which excludes a referent the child knows is elsewhere

options.text: The child is naming a category rather than an object, so the category rather than the toy is what is referred to
options.misconception: switches from a specific referent to a whole category without anything in the vignette licensing it

options.text: The child is about to point, since pointing always follows a first use of a word in a word-empty child
options.misconception: asserts a fixed order of pointing after speech that no evidence in the vignette supports

questions.explanation: The interesting feature of the vignette is that the two observers disagree, and the reason they do is supplied by the vignette itself: the referent is not in view from both positions. A word used for something outside the immediate field is exactly deferred reference, and it is a substantial thing for a word to do, because it requires the word to stand for something in its absence and a listener to accept that. That is the reading the correct option takes. The option that ties the referent to the gaze contradicts the second observer's report, since a patch of floor is not a car and cannot be what the child means. The category reading adds an assumption the vignette does not license, and nothing distinguishes naming the class from naming the instance here. The option about pointing asserts a fixed sequence that is not a finding, and the observers' disagreement is fully accounted for without it.
questions.hint: Ask why the two observers disagree, and whether that disagreement is consistent with the word naming what is in front of the child.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Languages in One Speaker, Counted Properly
questions.learningObjective: apply inclusion and exclusion to a bilingual vocabulary count
questions.stem: A speaker reports 1,500 words in one language and 1,200 words in the other, and says 700 of those words occur in both. First work out how many distinct words the speaker has in total across the two languages, then what share of that total is held in both.
questions.explanation: The two steps have to be done in that order because the share of a total is undefined until the total exists, and the total is not 1,500 plus 1,200 because that adds in the shared words twice. Inclusion and exclusion gives the count as 1,500 plus 1,200 minus 700, which is 2,000 distinct words. The share held in both is then 700 over 2,000, which is 0.35, so 35 percent. The wrong denominator is worth naming, because it is easy to fall into: dividing 700 by the sum 2,700 gives 25.9 percent, but 2,700 is not a count of anything, it double-counts the 700 shared words, so the ratio is comparing a subset with a number that contains that subset twice and will therefore always come out low. A third quantity also gets confused with these: the speaker knows 1,500 words in the first language and 1,200 in the second, so the overlap works out at 700 of 1,500, which is about 47 percent of the larger vocabulary and a different claim from the 35 percent.
questions.hint: Counting both lists and adding gives 2,700, but every shared word has been counted twice, so remove one copy of each of the 700 before dividing.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Where the Difficulty of a Sentence Lands in the Eye Record
questions.learningObjective: interpret where a reader's gaze pauses as evidence about processing difficulty
questions.stem: Eye movements are recorded while two groups read the same sentences. Group 1 reads sentences with no temporary ambiguity. Group 2 reads sentences containing a phrase that could attach either way. Group 2 spends markedly more time in the region where the attachment is decided, and the difference in that region is larger than the difference anywhere else in the sentence. Which conclusion does this support?

options.text: That the two groups read the sentences at different overall speeds, since a larger difference anywhere means a faster reader
options.misconception: reads a local difference in time as a global difference in reading speed

options.text: That the extra processing effort is concentrated where the structural decision is made, which is what the pattern of where the extra time falls indicates
That group 2 found the sentences harder to see, since more time on a region is a measure of how visible it was
options.misconception: treats fixation duration as a measure of visual salience rather than of processing

options.text: That group 2 misread every ambiguous sentence, since an increased processing time at a decision point can only follow a wrong decision
options.misconception: assumes extra processing at a decision point can only be the result of having decided wrongly

questions.explanation: The whole force of the design is in the phrase about where the difference falls. It is not just that one group took longer, which could be a general difference in speed; it is that the extra time is concentrated at the region where the structural decision has to be made, which is what localises the effort. That is what the correct option states. The option converting a local difference into a global speed difference discards the localisation, which is the informative part, and a general slowness would show a spread rather than a peak. The option treating time as visibility confuses two different things a fixation can reflect, and nothing in the design varies contrast or acuity. The option saying extra time can only follow an error overstates what the measure shows: an item can demand a decision, the decision can be made correctly, and the decision can still cost time.
questions.hint: Ask what the design varies and where in the sentence the difference appears.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Groups Judging Word Meaning, and What the Difference Shows
questions.learningObjective: run and interpret a two-sample comparison of response times
questions.stem: In a word-judgement task, 100 semantically related word pairs are judged and 100 unrelated pairs are judged. The mean time for related pairs is 480 ms with a standard deviation of 80 ms, and for unrelated pairs it is 520 ms with a standard deviation of 80 ms. Which reading of these figures is correct?

options.text: The 40 ms difference divided by the pooled standard deviation of 80 gives an effect size of 0.5, which is the same thing as the t statistic
options.misconception: confuses a standardised effect size with an unstandardised test statistic computed from a standard error

options.text: The difference of 40 ms is large enough to be read directly as an effect, since the two standard deviations do not overlap the difference
options.misconception: treats a raw difference as self-interpreting, which is what the standard error exists to prevent

options.text: The standard error of the 40 ms difference is about 11.3 ms, giving t of about 3.54 on 198 degrees of freedom and a p value below .001
The 40 ms difference cannot be evaluated at all, because the two groups were tested with different numbers of words
options.misconception: asserts the groups must be the same size, when the standard error handles unequal sizes

questions.explanation: The standard error of a difference between two means is the square root of the sum of the two variances over their sample sizes, which here is the square root of two times 80 squared over 100, giving 11.31 ms. The difference of 40 ms divided by 11.31 gives 3.54, and with 198 degrees of freedom the two-sided p value is about 0.0005, so comfortably below .001. That is the correct reading and the option states it. The effect-size option divides by the standard deviation rather than by the standard error, giving 0.5; that is a perfectly good measure of the effect in standard deviation units and it is not the t statistic, since the two differ by the square root of the sample size per group. The option treating the raw difference as self-interpreting makes the error the standard error exists to prevent. The option claiming unequal sizes make it unevaluable is simply false, since the standard error is defined for any two sample sizes.
questions.hint: Put both variances over their own sample sizes, add them, and take the square root before dividing the mean difference.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Sentence That Is Slow Because of One Structural Choice
questions.learningObjective: explain what an ambiguous sentence reveals about a listener's commitment
questions.stem: Readers are timed on 'The horse raced past the barn fell'. At the word 'fell' most readers take noticeably longer than on 'The horse raced past the barn was led'. Which explanation accounts for that difference?

options.text: In the first sentence the final word is longer to pronounce than the final word of the second, so the extra time is in production
options.misconception: attributes a comprehension-time difference to word length at the end of the sentence, which was not varied

options.text: In the first sentence the final verb is more ambiguous in meaning than a passive verb, so the reader is choosing between two meanings
options.misconception: makes the difficulty a matter of lexical ambiguity in the verb rather than of how earlier words attach

options.text: In the first sentence the two clauses must be compared for factual plausibility, so the reader is checking the story for coherence
options.misconception: requires a truth check on the content, which is not what sentence parsing involves

options.text: In the first sentence the earlier phrase can still be read as the subject of the final verb, so the reader must choose between two analyses at that point

questions.explanation: Both sentences end in a one-syllable verb, so pronunciation length cannot account for anything, which disposes of one option at once. What differs is the number of analyses still available at that word. In the first sentence the phrase before the final verb could be either a completed subordinate clause or a subject waiting for its verb, and the arriving verb forces a choice between those two, whereas the passive in the second sentence leaves the earlier phrase available as a subject without any competing reading being eliminated. That is the correct account and it is a statement about a decision point, not about speed or length. The option about lexical ambiguity misplaces the ambiguity, since the verb is ordinary and the trouble is in the arrangement of earlier words. The option requiring a plausibility check confuses parsing with comprehension, and a parser does not decide whether the horse actually fell.
questions.hint: Count how many ways the phrase before the final verb can still be read once that verb arrives.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Why a Rare Word Is Slow Even When It Is Predictable
questions.learningObjective: interpret a lexicality or frequency effect as evidence about processing
questions.stem: Listeners judge whether a string is a word. Judgements are slower and less accurate for strings that are rare in written text, even when the string is in a sentence that predicts it strongly. Which account does that pattern favour?

options.text: An account on which the word's familiarity contributes to processing over and above what the sentence context supplies
An account on which context is irrelevant, since a strong prediction should remove every source of difficulty
options.misconception: reads a residual effect as proof that context does nothing at all

options.text: An account on which the effect must be motor, since slow judgements require a different response from the two hands
options.misconception: invents a motor account for a judgement task that requires no motor response

options.text: An account on which rarity simply means the word has several meanings, so more meanings must mean more time
options.misconception: confuses frequency of occurrence in a corpus with number of distinct senses

questions.explanation: The design holds context strong and varies familiarity, and finds an effect anyway. An effect that survives the control is evidence that something beyond context is contributing, which is what the correct option says and what an account built only on prediction cannot produce. The option declaring context irrelevant makes a prediction the data contradict: if context did everything, familiarity would not matter once the context was strong. The motor option is unfounded, because judging whether a string is a word is a decision, not a response, and no hand has to do anything differently for a rare word. The option conflating corpus frequency with number of senses gets the construct wrong: rarity counts how often a form occurs in a body of text, and a word can be frequent with several senses or rare with only one.
questions.hint: Ask what was held constant across the conditions, and what an effect that survives that control implies.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Picture That Has Been Named Before It Is Shown
questions.learningObjective: interpret a priming effect and the inference it does not license
questions.stem: Participants see a picture that has previously been paired with a word, then see new objects and name them. Naming is faster for objects similar to the primed picture than for dissimilar ones. A control group sees no prior pairing. Which statement about the procedure is correct?

options.text: The prior pairing proves that the second exposure was a re-presentation of the first, since only re-presentation can speed a response
options.misconception: identifies faster responding with re-presentation, which is one of several possible carry-over effects

options.text: The prior pairing affected later performance, so something carried over from the first exposure; whether that something is a memory or an activated representation is not settled
The control group rules out an effect of the pictures themselves, so the difference must be entirely a property of the words
options.misconception: credits the control with ruling out a stimulus effect, when the control differs only in having no priming pair

options.text: The effect shows that naming a picture is a purely motor act, since the words contributed nothing to it
options.misconception: concludes a purely motor act from an effect of having earlier seen a word, which is not a motor manipulation

questions.explanation: The comparison establishes carry-over: performance on later objects depends on what was paired with something earlier, and the control group shows the difference is not simply a property of the pictures. What it does not establish is which of several carry-over mechanisms was responsible, because a prior pairing could raise the accessibility of a shared feature, could leave a trace that facilitates matching, or could change expectations about what is coming next. Naming the mechanism as settled is what the correct option avoids. The option equating faster responding with re-presentation identifies one possible account with the phenomenon. The option credits the control with more than it can do: it differs only in lacking the pairing, so it controls for the effect of the pictures but says nothing about which component of the pairing did the work. The option concluding a purely motor act contradicts its own premise, since a word pairing is not a motor manipulation.
questions.hint: Ask what the control group actually holds constant, and how many different mechanisms could produce a carry-over.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Two Word Kinds, Two Interference Effects
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the interference effect for word reading from that for colour naming
questions.stem: In one task participants name the colour of ink, and in another they read the word printed in that ink. In the first task a slow-down appears when the ink colour and the word disagree; in the second, a slow-down appears when the ink colour and the word agree. What explains the difference?

options.text: The two tasks differ only in the length of the words used, since longer words slow reading and leave colour naming unaffected
options.misconception: proposes a word-length account for a manipulation that is a colour-word conflict

options.text: The effect in the first task is a memory effect and the effect in the second is an attention effect, so they are not comparable
options.misconception: assigns the two effects to different mechanisms without evidence, since both arise from the same conflict

options.text: The task determines which information is automatic and which must be checked, so naming a colour cannot be overridden by the word but reading the word can be overridden by the ink
The second task shows no interference at all and the agreement condition is simply harder because the word is redundant
options.misconception: reads the agreement slow-down as an absence of interference rather than as interference in the other direction

questions.explanation: Both effects come from the same manipulation, a conflict between the ink and the word, and they differ because the two tasks demand different things of the reader. Naming the colour requires producing the colour word from the ink, and the meaning of the printed word is not what that task needs, so it gets in the way when they conflict. Reading the word is the opposite case: the printed word is what must be produced, so conflicting ink information is what has to be suppressed. That is the correct account, and it is why the direction of the interference flips. The word-length option is irrelevant to the manipulation, which is a conflict and not a length. The option assigning the two effects to unrelated mechanisms denies the obvious fact that they were produced by one manipulation. The option calling the agreement slow-down an absence of interference reverses the logic, since interference in the reading task runs from the ink rather than from the word.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two sources of information each task actually needs to produce, and which one therefore has to be ignored.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Damaged Area and the Loss It Produces
questions.learningObjective: relate a described lesion pattern to a specific language function
questions.stem: Damage to a region in the left hemisphere produces speech that is sparse and effortful. Word comprehension is largely intact, and the patient can repeat a phrase back accurately, but naming is hard and the grammar of sentences is simplified. Which description fits this pattern?

options.text: A receptive aphasia, in which understanding language is lost even though speech continues to flow easily
options.misconception: labels the pattern receptive, which reverses which of the two capacities is damaged

options.text: A global aphasia, in which production, comprehension and repetition are all lost to the same degree
options.misconception: claims all three capacities fail, while the vignette has two of them intact

options.text: An anomia, in which a word is understood and can be repeated but cannot be produced at all
options.misconception: narrows the difficulty to naming alone, ignoring the described effortful and simplified speech

options.text: An expressive aphasia, in which producing speech is impaired while comprehension and repetition are relatively preserved

questions.explanation: Three features in the vignette have to be read together rather than one at a time: speech is sparse and effortful, comprehension is largely intact, and repetition is accurate. Comprehension and repetition being spared is what makes this a production problem rather than a loss of language altogether, and the contrast with the receptive alternative is the key discriminator the item turns on. Effortful, grammatically simplified output with naming difficulty is the standard description of the pattern produced by damage to the region classically associated with speech production in the left hemisphere. That is the correct option. The receptive alternative is contradicted outright by the preserved comprehension. The global alternative is contradicted by the two preserved capacities. The anomia alternative picks out one feature and drops the rest, and it also overstates it, since anomia is difficulty finding the word while the surrounding speech continues, whereas here the speech itself is affected.
questions.hint: Read the three preserved and impaired features together, and ask which single label covers all of them.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: Speech That Flows but Cannot Be Checked Against Its Meaning
questions.learningObjective: relate a described lesion pattern to preserved speech with lost comprehension
questions.stem: A patient produces long, fluent, grammatical-sounding speech at a normal rate. Asked to repeat a sentence, the patient produces something fluent that does not match it. Asked what the sentence means, the patient gives a confident but unrelated answer. Which account best fits the pattern as described?

options.text: A receptive aphasia, in which speech production survives while comprehension and the matching of speech to meaning are impaired
An expressive aphasia, in which the effort devoted to producing speech is what makes the output short and simplified
options.misconception: describes effortful output, which is the opposite of the fluent effortless speech in the vignette

options.text: A conduction aphasia, in which repetition fails while comprehension and fluent speech both survive intact
options.misconception: claims comprehension survives, which the confident unrelated answers contradict

options.text: A global aphasia, in which every component of language has been lost together rather than selectively
options.misconception: asserts total loss, while the vignette describes fluent grammatical output

questions.explanation: The vignette describes three things at once and the correct label is the one that fits all three together: speech is fluent and effortless, repetition fails, and meaning is not available. Fluent production alongside lost comprehension and failed repetition is the pattern classically associated with damage to the region in the left hemisphere implicated in understanding language, and the confident wrong answers are part of the picture rather than an embarrassment to it, since the patient can produce sentences without a route from them to meaning. That is the correct option. The expressive alternative predicts effortful, shortened, simplified output, which is the opposite of what is described. The conduction alternative does get repetition wrong, which is the one feature it should be praised for, but it requires comprehension to be intact and the patient plainly cannot match speech to meaning. The global alternative requires everything to be lost, and fluent grammatical speech is plainly intact.
questions.hint: Take all three features at once: production, repetition, and comprehension.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Failure of Repetition That Locates the Problem
questions.learningObjective: explain what preserved repetition and lost comprehension together imply
questions.stem: A pattern is described in which comprehension of spoken language is impaired, speech is fluent, and repeating a heard phrase back accurately is also impaired. What does the failure to repeat, taken with the preserved fluency, indicate about the defect?

options.text: That the muscles of speech are damaged, since an accurate repetition is a motor act and cannot fail for any other reason
options.misconception: makes repetition failure a muscle diagnosis, ignoring that it is a linguistic operation

options.text: That the spoken input is not being converted into a form the speech system can copy, so the break lies between hearing the words and using them
That the patient has lost the meaning of the words entirely, which is why nothing can be repeated back
options.misconception: identifies repetition failure with loss of meaning, which the fluency of the patient's own speech argues against

options.text: That auditory acuity is impaired, since every language function listed would follow from not hearing well
options.misconception: explains a pattern-specific profile by a general sensory deficit, which would not spare the rest of language

questions.explanation: The combination is informative because it is selective. Fluency rules out a motor account, since the patient produces fluent grammatical speech effortlessly. Comprehension loss says the words are not being given their meaning. Repetition failure then adds the informative part: repeating a phrase is an operation that copies an input into an output form, and doing that accurately requires the input to have been held in a usable linguistic representation rather than merely registered acoustically. So the defect lies on the route from hearing the words to a representation the speech system can copy, which is what the correct option says. The motor option is ruled out by the fluency the pattern includes. The option equating repetition failure with total loss of meaning is ruled out by the patient's own meaningful speech, which shows meaning is available in production. The sensory option cannot produce a selective profile, since difficulty hearing would affect every language task rather than sparing fluency.
questions.hint: Ask what repetition requires beyond hearing, and which of the described capacities rules out each alternative.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: A Word That Cannot Be Found but Is Clearly Known
questions.learningObjective: describe anomia and separate it from a loss of word meaning
questions.stem: A patient is shown a picture of a watering can and says 'the thing you pour water with', describes exactly how it works, and can act it out. Asked a moment later what the object is called, the patient cannot produce the word but does not use a wrong word and does not claim not to know what it is. Which description fits?

options.text: Loss of the concept, since a patient who did not have it could not describe what the object is for
options.misconception: cannot be right, because the accurate functional description shows the concept is present

options.text: A word-form deafness, since the patient cannot map the sound of the name onto the object it names
options.misconception: describes a sound-to-object binding failure, when the patient recognises the object and its meaning perfectly well

options.text: Anomia, in which the concept and the surrounding speech are intact but access to the specific sound form fails on that occasion
A semantic dementia, since a progressive loss of meaning is the usual cause of this pattern
options.misconception: asserts a particular progressive condition from a single observation with nothing indicating progression

questions.explanation: The vignette is built so that everything except one step is demonstrated to work. The patient knows what the object is, describes its function accurately, and can mime its use, so the concept is intact and available to thought. What is missing is one particular item: the sound form of the name, on that occasion and without substitution by a wrong word. That is anomia, and it is a failure of access to a specific lexical item rather than a loss of the concept, which is why the correct option distinguishes the two. The concept-loss option is refuted by the accurate description. The sound-form option describes a different deficit, in which the connection between a heard sound and its referent is impaired, and the patient here has no such difficulty. questions.topic: Language: What Comprehension of a Single Word Requires
questions.learningObjective: order the stages that a route from print to meaning must pass through
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order they occur on the route from a printed word to what the word means.

options.text: The eye registers the pattern of marks on the page
Individual letters or letter groups are identified against stored shapes
The string of letters is matched to a word form held in memory
The word form's sounds are recovered, either from memory or by a letter-to-sound conversion
The word's meaning and its role in the sentence are recovered

questions.explanation: The keyed order is A, B, C, D, E, and the reasoning is that each stage hands something to the next. Retinal registration must come first because nothing about the marks is available until the image is formed. Letter identification depends on that, and it depends on stored representations of letter shapes, which is why it is a matching process and not a reading of the raw image. Matching the whole string to a word form comes next, because a reader usually recognises the word as a unit rather than decoding it letter by letter. Sound recovery follows from the word form, either by retrieving a stored pronunciation or by running a conversion, and those two routes can both be used. Only after the sound is available, or after the word is recognised directly, can the meaning and the grammatical role be recovered. The orderings that would put meaning before sound, or the whole word before its letters, each describe a process that is not the one the evidence supports.
questions.hint: Nothing about the marks is available before the image forms, and nothing about the word is available before its letters are identified.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Language: What a Design Comparing Two Groups of Speakers Cannot Show
questions.learningObjective: design a study that separates vocabulary from everything else about the speakers
questions.stem: A study reports that speakers of language A respond faster than speakers of language B to words whose meanings differ across the two languages, on a word-judgement task. Design a study that could attribute the finding to differences in vocabulary rather than to something else about the two groups, and say what it has to report.

answer.exemplar: The design has to break the confounding of language with person, because the reported finding is a difference between two groups of people and those groups differ in a great many respects besides the language they speak. Two designs do this. The cleanest uses the same people in both roles: recruit speakers who use both languages and test each of them on words whose senses agree across the two and on words whose senses differ, and measure the difference within speaker, so that person is held constant and the linguistic relation is what varies. The second design keeps between-group comparison but addresses the confounds by measuring rather than assuming them: match the groups on age, on years of schooling, on the amount of reading each language gets and on prior experience with a word-judgement task, exclude participants whose language histories differ in ways that cannot be aligned, and report the comparison variables so a reader can see how far the groups really were comparable. Either design should also hold constant what is not under investigation, so the same task, the same instructions in the same words, the same response format and the same number of trials, since a timing task is sensitive to the response and the finding would then be about the response rather than about the vocabulary. The stimulus sets need attention too: use the same concepts in both languages, and confirm that the differing words really are the differing ones rather than differing in familiarity or in length, because both of those affect word-judgement speed independently of meaning. Report the within-group differences with their spread rather than a single averaged figure, because a mean over people conceals the differences between them, and report how many participants were excluded and on what grounds, decided before the results were seen. Finally, say in advance what would count as evidence for the vocabulary account and what would count against it. If the effect tracks the linguistic relation within speakers, the vocabulary account is supported; if it tracks word familiarity or response format instead, the reported finding is about something other than vocabulary. A larger word list would not fix any of this, because a larger effect measured in a confounded design remains confounded.

questions.explanation: The answer has to name the confounding of language with person as the problem to be solved, give at least one design that solves it by holding the person constant or by measuring the confounds rather than assuming them, and insist on reporting the comparison variables and the exclusions. It should note that a larger stimulus set does not address the problem, since that is precision rather than validity, and it should close by specifying in advance what would count for and against the vocabulary account.
questions.hint: Ask what the two groups of speakers differ in besides their languages, and which design stops the finding being a difference between people.

questions.learningObjective: identify a design that would discriminate between two explanations of one result
questions.stem: Listeners recognise words faster when the word has been read aloud before than when it has not. One explanation is that a spoken presentation primes a phonological representation. A second is that it makes the item more familiar. What design would discriminate between them?

options.text: Present the prime in writing instead of speech, keeping the number of prior exposures matched, so familiarity is held while the spoken channel is removed
Add more spoken primes per item, since a stronger prime should produce a bigger effect if the phonological account is right
options.misconception: predicts that more exposure will separate the accounts, when both accounts predict that more exposure helps

options.text: Measure recognition speed for items never primed at all, since a baseline condition is what the two accounts are missing
options.misconception: assumes the accounts lack a baseline, when both predict faster recognition after any prior exposure

options.text: Use visually presented items throughout, since removing vision should stop the spoken prime from having any effect
options.misconception: changes a different channel entirely and so tests nothing about the prime

questions.explanation: Two explanations differ in what they predict will matter, so the discriminating design has to hold one constant while removing the other. The phonological account says the spoken channel is the active ingredient, so the prime must be spoken; the familiarity account says any prior exposure will do, so the channel should be irrelevant. Presenting the same prime in writing, with the number of prior exposures matched, holds familiarity fixed while removing the spoken channel. If the effect survives, familiarity is sufficient; if it disappears, the spoken channel was doing something. That is the correct design and it is the standard way to separate a channel-specific claim from a dose claim. The extra-exposure option fails because both accounts predict that more exposure produces more priming, so the prediction does not discriminate. The baseline option adds a condition both accounts already accommodate. The vision option alters a channel that neither account depends on, so it cannot bear on the difference between them.
